title: USPS Prints 20 Million Diwali Rangoli Stamps After Indian American Campaign
excerpt: The second USPS Diwali stamp in a decade was unveiled at the Indian Embassy in Washington, with a print run USPS set higher because of community advocacy and the first stamp's sales.
body:
• The US Postal Service has printed 20 million copies of its new Diwali Forever stamp, a run USPS called a little higher than usual because of strong Indian American advocacy for a second stamp.
  • The rangoli design is only the second Diwali stamp USPS has issued. The first, released in 2016, sold millions of copies.
  • Houston artist Sangita Bhutada created the rangoli over eight to 10 days. Photographer Bijay Dixit photographed the work for the stamp.
  • Readers can buy the stamp now in panes of 20 at post offices and through the USPS Postal Store. As a Forever stamp, it covers the current First-Class Mail one-ounce price.

The US Postal Service has printed 20 million copies of its new Diwali Forever stamp, unveiling the rangoli design at the Embassy of India in Washington on Wednesday. Shibani Gambhir, a USPS vice president who served as the dedicating official, told IANS the print run was set higher than usual because the Indian community had pushed hard for a second Diwali stamp and the first one had sold so well.

"There was so much advocacy on behalf of the Indian community to create a second stamp. And we just knew that this one was gonna be super popular like the first one, and hence we printed a little bit higher quantities for folks to enjoy."

— Shibani Gambhir, USPS vice president

"We have printed 20 million Rangoli stamps, and we're very excited for the Indian community to enjoy these," Gambhir said, adding that stamp collectors were also expected to buy the issue. The stamp is sold in panes of 20, according to the USPS announcement of the release.

A decade after the first Diwali stamp

The new issue is only the second stamp USPS has released for the festival of lights. The first came out in 2016. "The first stamp was wildly popular among the Indian community. We sold so many millions and millions of stamps," Gambhir said. Community groups campaigned for years for that first stamp, and the demand it generated shaped the scale of this second release.

https://x.com/yespunjab/status/2113152679795130554

India's Ambassador to the US, Vinay Mohan Kwatra, said the effort to partner with USPS on a Diwali stamp had been long in the making. "We attempted it last year; we were slightly delayed in catching up on the process, so we continued from last year," Kwatra said, according to The Indian Eye. He said the festival was first and foremost about "the millions of Indian Americans who call this country their home, students, professionals, the artists, families."

Kwatra described Indian Americans as a living bridge between the two countries. In an interview with IANS, he said the stamp was a chance "for us to celebrate our cultural strengths, our cultural heritage with the Indian American diaspora and with the larger US society here."

The artist behind the rangoli

The stamp features a rangoli by Sangita Bhutada, a native of India and a longtime Houston-area resident who has practised the folk art for nearly 30 years. Bhutada told IANS the work began with an email from USPS asking whether she could create a rangoli for a stamp. After signing a contract, she sent design sketches, then made the rangoli on the floor using starch-based coloured powder and coloured sand, sometimes with a kitchen strainer.

The finished work was 8 feet in diameter and took eight to 10 days, far longer than the four to six hours Bhutada normally spends on a rangoli, so it would photograph in high resolution. Her friend Bijay Dixit photographed the artwork. The image, in blue, orange, green, red and white, is set against a purple background. Jennifer Arnold designed the stamp and William J. Gicker served as art director, USPS said.

What readers can do

Diwali, observed by Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and others, marks the triumph of good over evil and is usually celebrated over five days. In 2026 the main day of the festival falls on Sunday, November 8, according to USPS. The Diwali stamp is a Forever stamp, so it will always equal the current First-Class Mail one-ounce price, even if postage rates rise later.

For Indian American families, the practical use is direct: the panes can be bought at post offices nationwide and through the USPS Postal Store for Diwali cards and festive mail sent in the run-up to November 8. Collectors can also order first-day-of-issue products through USPS philatelic channels listed in the release.

What happens next

USPS expects demand from both the community and collectors, based on the sales history of the 2016 stamp. Whether the 20 million print run is enough will be clear in the weeks around the festival, when Diwali mail and card-sending peak across the United States.
